issue.title: PowerShell autocompletion script fails with runtime errors on empty or single-item completions

relevant_locations.role: PowerShell completion script template containing the buggy array parsing and filtering logic

llm_context.input_title: PowerShell autocompletion script fails with runtime errors on empty or single-item completions
llm_context.input_body: No body provided in issue description.

generated_output.summary: The PowerShell autocompletion script generated by Cobra crashes with runtime errors when a command returns no completions or only a single completion. This happens because PowerShell automatically converts single-item arrays into scalar strings, causing index operations to return characters instead of strings, and because empty outputs lead to null-pointer exceptions.
generated_output.root_cause_analysis: In powershell_completions.go (lines 130-140), the script executes the completion command and stores the result in $Out. If the command fails or returns nothing, $Out is empty/null, and calling $Out[-1].TrimStart(':') fails. If the command returns exactly one line, PowerShell's pipeline unwraps the array into a scalar System.String. Accessing $Out[-1] on a string returns its last character (System.Char), which does not have a TrimStart method. Furthermore, using Where-Object { $_ -ne $Out[-1] } to remove the directive filters by value equality, which incorrectly strips any legitimate completion items that match the directive string.

step_by_step_plan.title: Inspect PowerShell Completion Template
step_by_step_plan.description: Locate the PowerShell completion script template in `powershell_completions.go` (specifically around the block handling `$Out`). Identify where `$Out` is populated and where `$Out[-1]` is accessed and filtered.

step_by_step_plan.title: Force Array Type and Handle Empty Output
step_by_step_plan.description: Modify the template to wrap the command invocation in `@(...)` (e.g., `$Out = @(...)`) to guarantee `$Out` is always treated as an array, even if it contains zero or one elements. Add a check to ensure `$Out.Length` is greater than 0 before attempting to process it.

step_by_step_plan.title: Safely Extract Directive and Slice Array
step_by_step_plan.description: Extract the last element of the array as the directive. Instead of using `Where-Object { $_ -ne $Out[-1] }` which filters out valid completions matching the directive value, slice the array to exclude the last element using `$Out = $Out[0..($Out.Length-2)]` when `$Out.Length` is greater than 1.

step_by_step_plan.title: Verify and Run Tests
step_by_step_plan.description: Add a test case in `completions_test.go` that verifies the generated PowerShell script handles empty completions and single-item completions without throwing errors. Run the test suite using the verified test command.

structured_concepts.short_explanation: PowerShell automatically unwraps single-element arrays into scalar objects (like a single String) when passed through pipelines or returned from expressions.
structured_concepts.why_it_matters: Developers writing PowerShell scripts must be aware of this behavior because indexing a scalar string ($Out[-1]) returns a System.Char instead of a System.String, which lacks string-specific methods like TrimStart.
structured_concepts.connection_to_issue: This unwrapping is the direct cause of the 'Method invocation failed because [System.Char] does not contain a method named 'TrimStart'' error when only one completion item is returned.

structured_concepts.short_explanation: Removing elements from an array should be done by index or position (e.g., using Select-Object -First) rather than filtering by value, unless value-based removal is explicitly desired.
structured_concepts.why_it_matters: Filtering by value can accidentally remove duplicate or identical legitimate data elements from a collection, whereas positional slicing guarantees only the intended element is removed.
structured_concepts.connection_to_issue: The current script uses Where-Object to filter out the directive, which accidentally removes any completion item that matches the directive's string value. Using Select-Object avoids this collision.

common_pitfalls: Assuming $Out is always a populated array of strings without checking its count or type.
Using value-based filtering (Where-Object) to remove a specific positional element (the last item) from a collection.
Forgetting that PowerShell's dynamic typing can convert arrays to scalars automatically, changing the behavior of index operators like [-1].
